{{Short description|Nilpotent subalgebra of a Lie algebra}}
{{Lie groups |Semi-simple}}

In [[mathematics]],  a '''Cartan subalgebra''', often abbreviated as '''CSA''', is a [[nilpotent Lie algebra|nilpotent]] [[subalgebra]] <math>\mathfrak{h}</math> of a [[Lie algebra]] <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> that is [[self-normalising]] (if <math>[X,Y] \in \mathfrak{h}</math> for all <math>X \in \mathfrak{h}</math>, then <math>Y \in \mathfrak{h}</math>). They were introduced by [[Élie Cartan]] in his doctoral thesis, and control the [[Representation theory of semisimple Lie algebras|representation theory of a semi-simple Lie algebra]] <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> over a field of characteristic <math> 0 </math>.

In a finite-dimensional [[semisimple Lie algebra]] over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero (e.g., {{nowrap|<math>\mathbb{C}</math>),}} a Cartan subalgebra is the same thing as a maximal abelian subalgebra consisting of elements ''x'' such that the [[adjoint endomorphism]] <math>\operatorname{ad}(x) : \mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{g}</math> is [[semisimple operator|semisimple]] (i.e., [[diagonalizable matrix|diagonalizable]]). Sometimes this characterization is simply taken as the definition of a Cartan subalgebra.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=Hotta, R. (Ryoshi)|title=D-modules, perverse sheaves, and representation theory|date=2008|publisher=Birkhäuser|others=Takeuchi, Kiyoshi, 1967-, Tanisaki, Toshiyuki, 1955-|isbn=978-0-8176-4363-8|edition=English|location=Boston|oclc=316693861}}</ref><sup>pg 231</sup>

In general, a subalgebra is called [[toral subalgebra|toral]] if it consists of semisimple elements. Over an algebraically closed field, a toral subalgebra is automatically abelian. Thus, over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, a Cartan subalgebra can also be defined as a maximal toral subalgebra.

[[Kac–Moody algebra]]s and [[generalized Kac–Moody algebra]]s also have subalgebras that play the same role as the Cartan subalgebras of semisimple Lie algebras (over a field of characteristic zero).<!-- But those are not called Cartan subalgebras at least in V. Kac, Infinite-dimensional Lie algebras. -->

== Existence and uniqueness ==
Cartan subalgebras exist for finite-dimensional Lie algebras whenever the base [[field (mathematics)|field]] is infinite. One way to construct a Cartan subalgebra is by means of a [[regular element of a Lie algebra#A Cartan subalgebra and a regular element|regular element]]. Over a finite field, the question of the existence is still open.{{citation needed|date=January 2020}}

For a finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak g</math> over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, there is a simpler approach: by definition, a [[toral subalgebra]] is a subalgebra of <math>\mathfrak g</math> that consists of semisimple elements (an element is semisimple if the [[adjoint endomorphism]] induced by it is [[diagonalizable matrix|diagonalizable]]). A Cartan subalgebra of <math>\mathfrak g</math> is then the same thing as a maximal toral subalgebra and the existence of a maximal toral subalgebra is easy to see.

In a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, all Cartan subalgebras are conjugate under [[automorphism]]s of the algebra, and in particular are all [[isomorphism|isomorphic]]. The common dimension of a Cartan subalgebra is then called the [[rank of a Lie algebra|rank]] of the algebra.

For a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra, the existence of a Cartan subalgebra is much simpler to establish, assuming the existence of a compact real form.<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} Chapter 7</ref> In that case, <math>\mathfrak{h}</math> may be taken as the complexification of the Lie algebra of a [[maximal torus]] of the compact group.

If <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is a [[linear Lie algebra]] (a Lie subalgebra of the Lie algebra of endomorphisms of a [[finite-dimensional vector space]] ''V'') over an algebraically closed field, then any Cartan subalgebra of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is the [[centralizer]] of a maximal [[toral Lie algebra|toral subalgebra]] of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>.{{citation needed|date=January 2020}} If <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is semisimple and the field has characteristic zero, then a maximal toral subalgebra is self-normalizing, and so is equal to the associated Cartan subalgebra.  If in addition <math>\mathfrak g</math> is semisimple, then the [[Adjoint representation of a Lie group|adjoint representation]] presents <math>\mathfrak g</math> as a linear Lie algebra, so that  a subalgebra of <math>\mathfrak g</math> is Cartan if and only if it is a maximal toral subalgebra.

== Examples ==

*Any nilpotent Lie algebra is its own Cartan subalgebra.
*The algebra of all diagonal matrices is a Cartan subalgebra of <math>\mathfrak{gl}_{n}</math>, the Lie algebra of [[square matrix|<math>n\times n</math> matrices]] over a field.{{citation needed|date=October 2020}}
*For the special Lie algebra of traceless <math>n\times n</math> matrices <math> \mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb{C})</math>, it has the Cartan subalgebra:<math display="block">\mathfrak{h} = \left\{ d(a_1,\ldots,a_n) \mid a_i \in \mathbb{C} \text{ and } \sum_{i=1}^n a_i = 0 \right\}</math> where <math display="block"> d(a_1,\ldots,a_n) = \begin{pmatrix}
a_1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
0   & \ddots &   & 0 \\
\vdots & & \ddots & \vdots \\
0   & \cdots & \cdots &a_n
\end{pmatrix}
</math> For example, in <math>\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb{C})</math> the Cartan subalgebra is the subalgebra of matrices:<math display="block"> \mathfrak{h} = \left\{
\begin{pmatrix}
a & 0 \\
0 & -a
\end{pmatrix} : a \in \mathbb{C}
\right\}</math> with Lie bracket given by the matrix commutator.
*The Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(\mathbb{R})</math> of <math>2</math> by <math>2</math> matrices of trace <math>0</math> has two non-conjugate Cartan subalgebras.{{citation needed|date=October 2020}}<!-- true but we need a ref. -->
*The dimension of a Cartan subalgebra is not in general the maximal dimension of an abelian subalgebra, even for complex simple Lie algebras. For example, the Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{sl}_{2n}(\mathbb{C})</math>of <math>2n</math> by <math>2n</math> matrices of trace <math>0</math> has a Cartan subalgebra of rank <math>2n-1</math> but has a maximal abelian subalgebra of dimension <math>n^{2}</math> consisting of all matrices of the form <math> \begin{pmatrix} 0 & A\\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}</math> with <math>A</math> any <math>n</math> by <math>n</math> matrix.  One can directly see this abelian subalgebra is not a Cartan subalgebra, since it is contained in the nilpotent algebra of strictly upper triangular matrices (or, since it is normalized by diagonal matrices).

== Cartan subalgebras of semisimple Lie algebras ==
{{see also|Semisimple Lie algebra#Structure}}
{{expand section|The action of the [[Weyl group]] on the algebra, as in the [[Harish-Chandra isomorphism]]|date=February 2014}}
For finite-dimensional [[semisimple Lie algebra]] <math>\mathfrak g</math> over an [[algebraically closed field]] of characteristic 0, a Cartan subalgebra <math>\mathfrak h</math> has the following properties:
*<math>\mathfrak h</math> is [[abelian Lie algebra|abelian]],
*For the adjoint representation <math>\operatorname{ad} : \mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{gl}(\mathfrak{g})</math>, the image <math>\operatorname{ad}(\mathfrak h)</math> consists of semisimple operators (i.e., diagonalizable matrices).
(As noted earlier, a Cartan subalgebra can in fact be characterized as a subalgebra that is maximal among those having the above two properties.)

These two properties say that the operators in <math>\operatorname{ad}(\mathfrak h)</math> are simultaneously diagonalizable and that there is a direct sum decomposition of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> as:
:<math>\mathfrak{g} = \bigoplus_{\lambda \in \mathfrak{h}^*} \mathfrak{g}_\lambda</math>
where 
:<math>\mathfrak{g}_\lambda = \{ x \in \mathfrak{g} : \text{ad}(h)x = \lambda(h)x, \text{ for } h \in \mathfrak{h}
\}</math>.

Let <math>\Phi = \{ \lambda \in \mathfrak{h}^* \setminus \{0\} | \mathfrak{g}_\lambda \ne \{0\} \}</math>. Then <math>\Phi</math> is a [[root system]] and, moreover, <math>\mathfrak{g}_0 = \mathfrak h</math>; i.e., the centralizer of <math>\mathfrak{h}</math> coincides with <math>\mathfrak{h}</math>. The above decomposition can then be written as:
:<math>\mathfrak{g} = \mathfrak{h} \oplus \left(
\bigoplus_{\lambda \in \Phi} \mathfrak{g}_\lambda
\right)</math>
As it turns out, for each <math>\lambda \in \Phi</math>, <math>\mathfrak{g}_{\lambda}</math> has dimension one and so:
:<math>\dim \mathfrak{g} = \dim \mathfrak{h} + \# \Phi</math>.

See also [[Semisimple Lie algebra#Structure]] for further information.

=== Decomposing representations with dual Cartan subalgebra ===
Given a Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> over a field of characteristic {{nowrap|<math>0</math>,}}{{clarify|Shouldn't it be semisimple?|date=October 2020}} and a [[Lie algebra representation]]<math display="block">\sigma: \mathfrak{g}\to \mathfrak{gl}(V)</math> there is a decomposition related to the decomposition of the Lie algebra from its Cartan subalgebra. If we set
<math display="block">V_\lambda = \{v \in V : (\sigma(h))(v) = \lambda(h) v \text{ for } h \in \mathfrak{h} \}</math>
with <math>\lambda \in \mathfrak{h}^*</math>, called the '''weight space for weight''' <math>\lambda</math>, there is a decomposition of the representation in terms of these weight spaces <math display="block">V = \bigoplus_{\lambda \in \mathfrak{h}^*} V_\lambda</math> In addition, whenever <math>V_\lambda \neq \{0\}</math> we call <math>\lambda </math> a '''weight''' of the <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>-representation {{nowrap|<math>V</math>.}}

==== Classification of irreducible representations using weights ====
{{main|Theorem of the highest weight}}
But, it turns out these weights can be used to classify the irreducible representations of the Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>. For a finite dimensional irreducible <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>-representation {{nowrap|<math>V</math>,}} there exists a unique weight <math>\lambda \in \Phi</math> with respect to a partial ordering on <math>\mathfrak{h}^*</math>. Moreover, given a <math>\lambda \in \Phi</math> such that <math>\langle \alpha, \lambda\rangle \in \mathbb{N}</math> for every positive root {{nowrap|<math>\alpha \in \Phi^+</math>,}} there exists a unique irreducible representation {{nowrap|<math>L^+(\lambda)</math>.}} This means the root system <math>\Phi</math> contains all information about the representation theory of {{nowrap|<math>\mathfrak{g}</math>.<ref name=":0" /><sup>pg 240</sup>}}

== Splitting Cartan subalgebra ==
{{main|Splitting Cartan subalgebra}}

Over non-algebraically closed fields, not all Cartan subalgebras are conjugate. An important class are [[splitting Cartan subalgebra]]s: if a Lie algebra admits a splitting Cartan subalgebra <math>\mathfrak{h}</math> then it is called ''splittable,'' and the pair <math>(\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{h})</math> is called a [[split Lie algebra]]; over an algebraically closed field every semisimple Lie algebra is splittable. Any two splitting Cartan algebras are conjugate, and they fulfill a similar function to Cartan algebras in semisimple Lie algebras over algebraically closed fields, so split semisimple Lie algebras (indeed, split reductive Lie algebras) share many properties with semisimple Lie algebras over algebraically closed fields.

Over a non-algebraically closed field not every semisimple Lie algebra is splittable, however.

== Cartan subgroup ==
{{For|a Cartan subgroup of a linear algebraic group|Cartan subgroup}}

The [[Lie group–Lie algebra correspondence]] allows one to translate the notion of Cartan subalgebras to Lie groups. Specifically, a subgroup <math>G\subset H</math> of a [[Lie Group]], translates to a sub Lie Algebra <math>Lie(G)\subset Lie(H) </math>. 

In the case of compact connected Lie groups, cartan subgroups are maximal connected [[Abelian group|Abelian subgroups]] and are oftentimes referred to as ‘[[maximal torus| maximal tori]].’

In the case of disconnected compact lie groups, there are two common definitions.
The '''large Cartan subgroup''' is defined as the group of elements that normalize a fixed [[maximal torus]] and fix the [[fundamental Weyl chamber]].
The '''small Cartan subgroup''' is defined as the centralizer of a maximal torus.

For any of these definitions, a cartan subgroup of a Lie group implies a Cartan subalgebra relation for the corresponding Lie algebras.


===Examples of Cartan Subgroups===
* The subgroup in GL<sub>2</sub>('''R''') consisting of diagonal matrices.
